newsitem.title: PERU: Churchman in shuttle diplomacy to end Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Churchman in shuttle diplomacy to end Peru crisis.

text.p: Roman Catholic Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani held a frenetic series of meetings on Tuesday aimed at finding a peaceful solution to Peru's 119-day-old hostage crisis.

Cipriani -- one of three guarantors overseeing talks to end the siege at the Japanese ambassador's home where Marxist rebels hold 72 hostages -- met with Peruvian government negotiator Domingo Palermo for more than an hour.

The 51-year-old archbishop rushed from that meeting to a 20-minute pit stop with Tokyo's crisis point man, Terusuke Tarada, that left Japanese Embassy officials catching their breath. They said they found out about the meeting when local radio reported that Cipriani had left.

The churchman then moved on to the siege site to try to persuade Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leaders to free their captives. Another member of the guarantors panel, Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent, followed him.
Tuesday's meetings followed Cipriani's four hours of dicussions on the crisis late on Monday with President Alberto Fujimori.
Cipriani offered no comments after any of the meetings.
While there have been no signs that his energetic shuttle diplomacy is making any progress, the guarantor insisted last week that advances were being made.

The rebels originally seized more than 500 guests after storming a cocktail party at Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki's home on Dec 17. They later released most of them, hanging on to a group including Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio, two Peruvian government ministers, two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and Fujimori's younger brother.

The rebels refuse to sit down for face-to-face negotiations with Palermo until they have concrete concessions over their main demand -- the release of their jailed comrades in exchange for the hostages' freedom -- a demand Fujimori publicly refuses to consider.
But sources close to the talks say the closed-door meetings are zeroing in on the issue and the two sides have begun haggling over specific prisoners to be freed.
Fujimori met on Tuesday with two members of Tokyo's special diplomatic team sent to Lima for the crisis, continuing his efforts to resolve the toughest problem of his seven years in office.
But in keeping with his line that despite the crisis Peru is going about its business as usual, Fujimori left Government Palace to inaugurate a new factory on the outskirts of Lima.
